Tantalum

Tantalum is a chemical element with the symbol Ta and atomic number 73. It is a rare, hard, blue-gray, lustrous transition metal that is highly corrosion-resistant. It is part of the refractory metals group.

Tantalum was discovered in Sweden in 1802 by Anders Ekeberg. It was initially confused with niobium, a closely related metal, until German chemist Heinrich Rose proved in 1844 that the two were distinct.

Applications

Tantalum is used in the electronics industry primarily for capacitors and in high-power resistors. Its biocompatibility also makes it useful in surgical instruments and orthopaedic implants.

Production

The largest producers of tantalum ore include the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Brazil, and Australia. Concerns about ethical sourcing have led to certification schemes for "conflict-free" tantalum supplies.
